title: Accepted proposal: grow an existing map with maps.Grow
summary: The maps package is getting a Grow function that presizes a map you already have, and maps.Copy will start doing it for you.
content:
Liz Fong-Jones’s proposal to add maps.Grow was accepted on October 29. It lets you make room in a map that already exists. make(M, n) already does this for a new map.

A Go map grows on its own as you add entries. When it runs out of room, the runtime allocates a larger hash table and rehashes the entries into it. The old table is left for the garbage collector. A loop that adds thousands of entries can hit this again and again. Each time costs CPU and creates more garbage. If you know the final size up front, you can pass it to make and skip all that extra work.

But that only works if you’re the one creating the map. If someone else created it and you only add entries, you can’t control how often it grows.

net/http/httputil.ReverseProxy hits this on every request. It copies the upstream response headers into the client’s response:

func copyHeader(dst, src http.Header) {
    for k, vv := range src {
        for _, v := range vv {
            dst.Add(k, v)
        }
    }
}

The proxy calls this as copyHeader(rw.Header(), res.Header). Here res is the upstream response and rw is the http.ResponseWriter for the client. rw.Header() returns the header map the server will send back to the client. The server created that map before the proxy’s code ran. The proxy knows how many headers are coming but can’t pass that number to the map. So the map may grow several times inside this loop.

The proxy can’t replace the map behind rw.Header(), so it’s stuck with this. Code that owns its map has a workaround. It can build a bigger map and swap it in. Honeycomb’s Go SDK, libhoney-go, does this. It keeps an event’s fields in a map and returns that map from Fields(). A simplified version looks like this:

type fieldHolder struct {
    data map[string]any
}

// Fields returns a reference to the event's field map.
func (f *fieldHolder) Fields() map[string]any {
    return f.data
}

func (f *fieldHolder) AddFields(src map[string]any) {
    if len(src) > len(f.data) {
        m := make(map[string]any, len(f.data)+len(src))
        maps.Copy(m, f.data) // (1)
        maps.Copy(m, src)
        f.data = m // (2)
        return
    }
    maps.Copy(f.data, src)
}

Here:

  • (1) copies every field that f.data already has into the bigger map
  • (2) swaps in the new map. Callers who got the old map from Fields() won’t see the new fields.

Even with the extra copy, adding this swap cut CPU use by about 5% in production. Copying everything once was cheaper than letting the map grow step by step.

With maps.Grow, you can skip all those shenanigans. It’s defined as:

// Grow increases m's capacity, if necessary, so that at least n more
// entries can be added without further growth in the typical case, as if
// m had been created with make(M, len(m)+n). Grow never shrinks m.
// This is best effort: it cannot guarantee there will be no additional
// growth.
//
// Grow panics if n is negative. It also panics if m is nil and n > 0,
// as assigning to an element of a nil map would.
func Grow[M ~map[K]V, K comparable, V any](m M, n int)

Using Grow, the proxy can make room before the loop starts:

func copyHeader(dst, src http.Header) {
    maps.Grow(dst, len(src))
    for k, vv := range src {
        for _, v := range vv {
            dst.Add(k, v)
        }
    }
}

libhoney can grow f.data in place. Callers who got the map from Fields() still hold that same map and see the new fields:

func (f *fieldHolder) AddFields(src map[string]any) {
    maps.Grow(f.data, len(src))
    maps.Copy(f.data, src)
}

If you’ve used slices.Grow, you might expect maps.Grow to return the grown map. It doesn’t, because Go stores slices and maps differently:

  • A slice is a small slice struct with a pointer to an array, a length, and a capacity. When slices.Grow needs more room, it makes a bigger array and copies the elements into it. Your old slice still points to the old array. That’s why you write s = slices.Grow(s, n).
  • A map is a pointer to a maps.Map struct in the runtime. When maps.Grow needs more room, it swaps the hash tables behind that pointer for larger ones. The pointer stays the same. Every variable holding the map sees the new tables, so there’s nothing to return.

A nil map is a nil pointer with no table behind it. That’s why Grow panics on a nil map when n > 0:

var m map[string]int // m is a nil map
maps.Grow(m, 0)  // fine, nothing to add
maps.Grow(m, 10) // panic: assignment to entry in nil map
maps.Grow(m, -1) // panic: maps: cannot grow by a negative count

If you don’t have a map yet, use make.

The doc comment also calls Grow best effort. Like the size you pass to make, n is only a hint. The map may still grow later. The comment mentions m’s capacity, but Go gives you no way to read it. An earlier proposal to allow cap on maps was declined.

Note

With a slice, cap(s) tells you exactly how far you can append before Go allocates a new array. A map can’t tell you that. A large map is split into several hash tables, and each key’s hash decides which table it goes into. One table can fill up and grow while the others still have room. A table also grows before all its slots are full. So cap(m) could only be a rough guess. That’s why Grow takes a hint and never reports a number back.

The proposal also changes maps.Copy.

Important

maps.Copy(dst, src) will now make room in dst for len(src) entries before it copies anything. That room never goes to waste, because dst holds at least len(src) entries after the copy. Code that already calls maps.Copy gets faster without any change. In the benchmarks, copying into an empty or small map took about half the time on an AMD 5600X. It also allocated about half as much memory.

maps.Copy makes room for len(src) entries in total. It doesn’t add room on top of what dst already holds. libhoney’s map has fields of its own, so it still calls Grow to make room for both. The proxy’s copyHeader doesn’t use maps.Copy at all. It adds headers one by one with Header.Add, so it needs its own Grow call. The same goes for code that fills a map from a slice:

func index(dst map[string]User, users []User) {
    maps.Grow(dst, len(users))
    for _, u := range users {
        dst[u.ID] = u
    }
}

If most of those users are already in dst, the extra room goes unused. You’ve spent memory for nothing.

The implementation, the Copy change, and a follow-up that uses maps.Grow in httputil and cgi are all still under review. They’re expected to land in Go 1.28.
